title: The Fresh Water Habitat
summary: Lotic and lentic fresh waters, their characteristics, the plants and animals and their adaptations, and fresh water food chains.

sections.h: What is a fresh water habitat?
p: A fresh water habitat is a body of water that comes mainly from inland sources and contains very little or no salt. There are two types, based on movement.
Lotic fresh waters are running waters that flow in one direction: rivers, streams and springs.
Lentic fresh waters are still (stagnant) waters that do not flow: lakes, ponds, puddles, swamps and dams.
1. It contains little or no salt (salinity about 0.5 parts per thousand; the source notes say 5 parts per thousand, or 0.5%, which is too high).
2. It is small compared with the sea.
3. It is rich in oxygen, especially near the surface and where water is moving.
4. It is often shallow, so sunlight reaches the bottom.
5. The temperature changes with the seasons and with depth.
6. There are seasonal changes: the water level falls or the pond dries up in the dry season and rises in the rainy season.
7. Currents affect the distribution of organisms, salts and gases, especially in rivers and streams.

Water lily has air spaces (air bladders) in its stalks and leaves, and broad, flat, light leaves that keep it afloat. Spirogyra has a slimy (mucilaginous) covering that protects it. Water lettuce has hairs on its leaves that trap air to keep it afloat. Elodea (a water weed) has long, flexible stems and leaves that sway with the water current.

Protozoa such as Amoeba and Paramecium have a contractile vacuole that pumps out the water that enters by osmosis (osmoregulation). Ducks have webbed feet for swimming and a flat (serrated) beak for sieving food from water. Hydra has a sticky base (or adhesive disc) and tentacles with stinging cells for attaching and catching food. Pond skaters have long legs that spread their weight so they can skate on the surface. Fishes have gills for breathing, fins for swimming and swim bladders for buoyancy.
Diatoms → fish fry → tilapia. Spirogyra → tadpole → carp → kingfish. Algae → mosquito larva → small fish.

title: Terrestrial Habitats: Marsh and Forest
summary: The four terrestrial habitats, the formation, characteristics and organisms of a marsh, and the rain forest: characteristics, plants, animals and food chains.

p: Terrestrial organisms live on and under the ground. There are four main terrestrial habitats: marsh, forest, grassland (savanna) and arid land (desert).

A marsh is low-lying land that is flooded in the rainy season and is usually waterlogged because of poor drainage. Grasses and shrubs are the main vegetation. When trees grow in it, it is called a swamp. A marsh is a transition between aquatic and terrestrial habitats.

Formation: marshes develop when water overflows river banks onto low coastal land or flood plains, helped by heavy rain. They also form when ponds and lakes slowly fill up with soil and plant remains, so the process is gradual. Marshes may be fresh water marshes or salt water marshes.
Characteristics: it is low land; it is wet, flooded and waterlogged; it may have pools of standing water; relative humidity is high; the water contains much decaying matter and often smells foul.

Organisms: plants include algae, grasses, water lettuce, water lilies, red and white mangrove and raffia palms. Animals include mangrove crabs, hermit crabs, mudskippers, fishes, frogs, snakes, crocodiles and some mammals.

Adaptations: organisms must tolerate the salt in soil or water in salt marshes, and the low oxygen in the soil or water. Plants of fresh water marshes have adaptations like those of fresh water plants. Saprophytic bacteria must live without oxygen (anaerobically).
Food chains: flowering plants → insects → frogs → crocodiles. Humus → earthworms → frogs → snakes.

A forest is a community of plants in which trees are the dominant plants. The kinds of forest depend mainly on temperature, rainfall, soil and human activities such as farming, logging, bush burning, road building and house building. The main type in southern Nigeria is the tropical rain forest.

Characteristics of a rain forest: it is rich in climbers and epiphytes; the inside is humid and damp with little light; the trees are tall and form layers (stratification) with a thick canopy; the trees are mesophytes with broad leaves; the trees have buttress roots to support their great weight and height; the barks are thin.

Forest plants include African walnut, mahogany, teak, obeche, iroko, oil palm, ferns, mosses and liverworts, orchids (epiphytes), fungi and mistletoe. Adaptations: strong tap roots and buttress roots; tall, unbranched trunks that reach for light; broad leaves to catch the little light that gets through; epiphytes have aerial roots that absorb moisture from the air while growing on the branches of trees; mistletoe is a partial parasite whose roots penetrate the stem of its host to take water and food from it.

Most forest animals are arboreal: bats, monkeys, squirrels, birds, snakes, tree frogs and chameleons. Some live in the soil (earthworms, beetles) and some in the leaf litter (millipedes, ants, snails). Adaptations: monkeys have long limbs and prehensile tails for climbing and jumping; bats have wings for flight; green snakes have colours that match leaves (camouflage); the chameleon has a prehensile tail, grasping digits and camouflage; apes live in groups for safety and have keen sight; earthworms and snails have moist skin or shells that reduce water loss; birds have strong wings.
Green plants → grasshopper → toad → hawk. Green plants → monkey → leopard. (The source notes give 'lion' as the predator of monkeys. Leopards, not lions, live in the forest.)

title: Grassland (Savanna)
summary: The meaning and characteristics of grassland, the types of savanna in Nigeria, and the plants and animals of the savanna with their adaptations and food chains.

p: Grassland (savanna) is a plant community in which grasses are the dominant plants, though trees and shrubs may be present.
1. The temperature is high and the sunshine is strong.
2. The relative humidity is low and rainfall is moderate to low (about 60 to 150 cm a year, in one season).
3. There is plenty of grass with a few short trees spread out here and there.
4. Bush fires are common, and the trees are fire-resistant.
5. Many plants are deciduous: they shed their leaves in the dry season.
6. Plants have underground stems and deep roots to find water.
7. Trees have small or modified leaves to cut down water loss.
There are four major types, from south to north: Southern Guinea savanna, Northern Guinea savanna, Sudan savanna and Sahel savanna. The Guinea savanna is the largest vegetation zone in Nigeria.

Plants include acacia, elephant grass, guinea grass, spear grass, palms and baobab trees. Adaptations: thick, corky bark that resists fire; grasses with underground stems that survive fire and drought; leaves with a waxy surface (thick cuticle) that cut down water loss; small or curled leaves that reduce transpiration; leaves that fall in the dry season (deciduous); the baobab has thick, spongy trunk that stores water.

Animals include antelopes, elephants, giraffes, zebras, goats, cattle, grasshoppers, lizards, birds, lions, leopards, rats, snakes and grasscutters. (The source notes also list tigers and kangaroos; tigers live in Asia and kangaroos in Australia, not in the Nigerian savanna.) Adaptations: termites build mounds that keep their nests cool; rats and other small animals burrow to escape the heat and fires; zebras and giraffes have patterned coats that make them hard to see in tall grass; lions and leopards have powerful claws and teeth for hunting; elephants, zebras and antelopes move in herds for safety in numbers; many grazers are fast runners with long legs.

title: Arid Land (Desert)
summary: The meaning and types of desert, its characteristics, and how its plants and animals are adapted, with food chains.

p: Arid lands (deserts) have very low rainfall (less than about 25 cm a year) and a high rate of evaporation. They are the driest habitats. There are hot deserts, such as the Sahara in North Africa and the Kalahari in southern Africa, and cold deserts, such as parts of Asia and North America.
1. Water is very scarce.
2. The temperature is very high by day and very low at night.
3. The vegetation is very thin and scattered.
4. The soil is sandy or rocky and has little humus.
5. Strong winds blow often and the sunshine is very strong.
6. The plants are drought-resistant (xerophytes).

Desert plants include thorny bushes, cacti, dwarf acacia, date palm, wiry grasses, baobab and euphorbia. Adaptations: small or thin leaves, or leaves reduced to spines, which cut down transpiration; fleshy (succulent) stems that store water, as in cactus; deep roots that reach underground water, as in acacia; a thick waxy cuticle and sunken pores (stomata); narrow, slender leaves in wiry grasses; many seeds that stay dormant in the soil until it rains.

Animals include camels, rodents, lizards, snakes, desert tortoises, grasshoppers, wasps, ants and scorpions. Adaptations: most produce very dry droppings and concentrated urine to save water; rats and other small animals stay in burrows by day and come out at night; reptiles have dry scaly skin that reduces water loss; the camel can go many days without drinking, stores fat in its hump, and can tolerate a rise in body temperature; broad padded feet stop it sinking in sand; locusts and insects have waterproof cuticles. (The source notes list zebras as desert animals; zebras live in savanna.)
Plants → desert rat → snake. Plants → ants → scorpion → snake.

title: Reproduction: Meaning and Types of Asexual Reproduction
summary: What reproduction is, asexual and sexual reproduction, and the types of asexual reproduction: binary fission, budding, spore formation, fragmentation, vegetative propagation, parthenogenesis and schizogony.

p: Reproduction is the process by which living organisms produce new individuals (offspring) of their own kind. It keeps a species from dying out.

Asexual reproduction: one parent produces offspring without gametes (sex cells) and without the joining of nuclei. The offspring are clones: they are genetically identical to the parent. It is common in single-celled organisms, in flowering plants and in organisms that can reproduce both ways depending on conditions such as food and environment.
Sexual reproduction: offspring are produced by the joining (fusion) of two different sex cells, usually from two different parents. The offspring differ from their parents and from each other.

Binary fission: the parent divides by mitosis into two (or more) parts, each able to live alone. It occurs in bacteria and in protists such as Amoeba and Paramecium. Division into many parts is called multiple fission.
Budding: the offspring grows as an outgrowth (bud) of the parent and later breaks off to live on its own. It occurs in Hydra, yeast and corals. Some sponges form internal buds.
Spore formation: spores are tiny, light cells produced in large numbers and spread by wind. They are produced by fungi (Mucor, Rhizopus), mosses, ferns, algae, some protists and some bacteria.
Fragmentation: a part of the organism breaks off and grows into a new one. It occurs in Spirogyra, some algae, planarians and sponges.
Vegetative propagation: in higher plants a new plant grows from part of the old plant other than the seed, such as a stem, root or leaf (for example, yam tubers, cassava stems, sweet potato).
Parthenogenesis: an embryo develops from an unfertilised egg cell. It occurs in aphids, honey bees, ants, wasps, and some fish, amphibians and reptiles. (The source notes spell it 'patogenesis'.)

Schizogony: a form of multiple fission in which a parasite divides many times inside its host. The malaria parasite Plasmodium multiplies in this way in the liver and red blood cells, giving merozoites.

title: Reproduction in Amoeba, Paramecium and Spirogyra
summary: Binary and multiple fission in amoeba, fission and conjugation in paramecium, and fragmentation and conjugation in spirogyra.

p: Amoeba reproduces asexually by binary fission and, in bad conditions, by multiple fission (sporulation).
Binary fission: when an amoeba has grown to full size it stops moving. The nucleus divides first by mitosis, then the cytoplasm divides, giving two daughter amoebae.

Multiple fission: in bad conditions the amoeba becomes round and makes a hard cover (a cyst) around itself. Inside the cyst, the nucleus divides many times. When conditions improve the cyst bursts, and each nucleus, with a bit of cytoplasm, becomes a small new amoeba.

img.alt: Four stages of binary fission in an amoeba: parent cell, nucleus dividing, cytoplasm dividing, two daughter cells

p: Paramecium reproduces asexually by binary fission and sexually by conjugation.

Binary fission: in good conditions the micronucleus divides by mitosis, the macronucleus (the 'meganucleus' in the source notes) lengthens and splits, and the cell constricts across the middle into two new paramecia.

Conjugation: two paramecia of different strains come together and join at their oral grooves. In each one the micronucleus divides twice by meiosis to give four nuclei, and three of them break down. The remaining nucleus divides once more into a migratory nucleus and a stationary nucleus. The migratory nuclei are exchanged through the joined cells. Each migratory nucleus then fuses with the stationary nucleus of its partner to form a new (zygote) nucleus. The two paramecia separate. In each, the new nucleus divides three times to give eight nuclei; four become macronuclei and four become micronuclei. The cell then divides to give four young paramecia, each with one macronucleus and one micronucleus. Conjugation exchanges genetic material, so it adds variety.
Spirogyra is a green alga that forms long, thread-like filaments. It reproduces asexually by fragmentation and sexually by conjugation.
Fragmentation: when a filament has grown long, parts break away and each grows into a new filament.

Conjugation: (1) two filaments lie side by side and cells grow tubes towards each other, forming conjugation tubes; (2) the contents of cells in one filament act as the male gamete and the cells of the other filament as the female; (3) the male gamete passes through the tube and fuses with the female gamete to form a zygote; (4) the zygote forms a thick, resistant wall and is called a zygospore; (5) after a resting period, in good conditions, the wall bursts and a new filament grows.

title: Reproduction in the Earthworm and the Cockroach
summary: How earthworms copulate and produce cocoons, and how cockroaches mate, lay egg cases and develop by incomplete metamorphosis.

p: Earthworms are hermaphrodites: each worm has both male and female sex organs and makes both male and female gametes. Reproduction is sexual. Each worm gives sperm to the other (cross-fertilisation).

Copulation: two worms come together at night outside their burrows and lie with their ventral (under) surfaces touching, facing opposite ways. The reproductive organs are near the front of the body. The segments carrying the male openings (about segments 9 to 15 in the notes) of one worm lie against the clitellum (the thick, smooth band, about segments 32 to 37 in the notes) of the other. The worms are held together by their bristles (chaetae) and by mucus. Sperm pass from one worm to the other and are stored.

After copulation the worms separate. The clitellum makes a ring of mucus (a cocoon) which slides forward over the body, picking up eggs and then the stored sperm so that fertilisation takes place inside the cocoon. The cocoon slips off the head and closes at both ends. The embryos develop inside the cocoon, and young worms hatch out. Only one or a few worms hatch from each cocoon.

Cockroaches reproduce sexually and fertilisation is internal. The male and female mate and the male puts sperm into the female's genital opening. The sperms are stored in a sperm pouch until the eggs are released from the two ovaries; they are fertilised as they come out.

The eggs (about 10 to 16) are laid in a hard, horny egg case called an ootheca, which the female carries at the end of her abdomen for some time and then drops in a safe, dark place. After 30 to 100 days the eggs hatch into nymphs. Nymphs are small, wingless and whitish, and look like small adults.

The nymphs feed and grow and turn brown. They moult (shed their skin) about 13 times. At each moult they get bigger, and wings first show as wing pads and then grow into full wings in the adult (the imago). It takes about 11 to 20 months from egg to adult. The change from egg to adult has no pupa stage, so this is incomplete metamorphosis (gradual change).

title: Reproduction in the Housefly and the Snail
summary: The life cycle of the housefly (complete metamorphosis) and reproduction in land snails, including torsion.

p: The adult male and female mate and, within two to three days, the female lays fertilised eggs, by day, in moist, dirty places such as rubbish and dung. A female lays 2 to 7 batches of about 100 to 150 eggs. The housefly has complete metamorphosis: egg, larva, pupa, adult.
Egg: the eggs hatch into larvae in about 8 to 24 hours.

Larva (maggot): a white, legless, segmented body with a pointed head that bears a pair of hooks for tearing food and pulling the maggot along. Spiny pads on the underside help it to move, and it breathes through two pairs of spiracles. It feeds, grows and moults several times over about 5 to 14 days, then crawls to a dry place.

Pupa: the maggot shortens and its skin hardens and turns brown, forming a case called the puparium. The pupa does not feed or move. Inside, the body is rebuilt into the adult form. This takes about 3 to 10 days.
Adult (imago): the adult breaks out of the puparium by blowing up a bladder-like sac on its head (the ptilinum). It crawls to the surface of the rubbish and flies away when its wings have dried.

img.alt: Life cycles of the housefly (egg, larva, pupa, adult) and the cockroach (egg case, nymph, adult)
img.cap: Complete metamorphosis in the housefly, compared with the incomplete metamorphosis of the cockroach (Unit 15).

p: Houseflies feed on rubbish and faeces and then land on our food. They carry the microbes of cholera, typhoid, dysentery and polio on their legs and bodies, and in their droppings and vomit. This is why we cover food and keep refuse and toilets clean.

Land snails are hermaphrodites, and fertilisation is internal. Two snails mate and exchange sperm packets (spermatophores). Sperm are passed into the partner's body, are stored and travel to the place where fertilisation takes place. (The source notes name several parts of the sperm duct such as the epiphallus and the bursa duct.) The fertilised eggs are laid in a hole in damp soil.

During the development of a snail, the visceral mass (the soft body part holding the organs) twists through 180°. This brings the anus and the mantle cavity forward to a place above the head. This twisting is called torsion.
